svg.text: The rotary knob (EC11) close up: it is three switches in one
Two switches click on and off as you turn it (A and B), and one closes when you push it (SW). Each leg just connects or doesn't. No chips, no power needed.
this side: 3 legs, the turning part
the other side (behind): 2 legs, the push switch
3 legs in a row: A, C (always the middle), B
2 legs: the push switch (they're the same, either way round)
Counts backwards? Swap the A and B wires.
Nothing can break either way: the Pico's own
pull-ups hold each pin high, and a closed switch
pulls it to ground. No resistors needed.
Inside, A and B each touch C in some positions and not in others. They take turns, a quarter step apart, so the Pico can tell which way you turned by which one moves first.
Each click you feel is one full cycle: 4 changes. The Pico reads them as high (switch open) and low (switch closed to ground).
Push: the two SW legs touch while you hold the shaft down. That is all the button is.
- Female-to-male jumper wires: the socket end pushes onto a leg, the pin end goes in the breadboard.
If one is loose, squeeze the socket gently with pliers, or tin the leg with a little solder.
- Or plug the knob itself into a spare end of the breadboard across the middle gap:
bend the two side tabs flat first; then wire from the legs' columns like any other part.
- Keep the legs from touching each other or the metal frame.
Five labelled pins, the switch ground already joined on the board.
